title: What Can We Know About the Beginning?
summary: Before asking how the universe began, we need to understand what observations can tell us, how far back astronomy can look, and where our knowledge reaches its limits.
body:
## The question behind every other question

Look up at the night sky and you are looking into the past. Moonlight takes a little over a second to reach Earth. Sunlight takes about eight minutes. Light from distant galaxies may have travelled for billions of years before it reaches a telescope.

That simple fact gives astronomy an unusual advantage: the universe carries a record of its own history. By collecting light, measuring how it has changed, and comparing observations with physical laws, scientists can reconstruct much of the story of the cosmos.

But there is a difference between learning about the early universe and knowing exactly what happened at the very beginning. The first is something science has made remarkable progress on. The second remains an open problem.

![Hubble eXtreme Deep Field showing thousands of distant galaxies](https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/cds/general/images/2023/07/hubble-xdf.jpg)

*The Hubble eXtreme Deep Field reveals thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky. Credit: NASA, ESA, and the XDF team. [Image details](https://science.nasa.gov/image-detail/amf-aced1866-f488-49ff-885e-8bff652febd3/).*

## What does “the beginning” mean?

When cosmologists talk about the beginning, they usually mean the early stages of the universe's expansion from a much hotter, denser state. The leading scientific model describes a universe that has been expanding and cooling for about 13.8 billion years.

This does not mean that scientists have found a point in space where everything exploded outward into empty surroundings. The Big Bang model describes space itself expanding. On very large scales, distant galaxies move away from one another because the space between them grows.

It is also important not to assume that the phrase “beginning of the universe” automatically tells us what, if anything, came before it. Our best-tested equations do not yet provide a complete account of the earliest possible moment.

## The observable universe is not the whole universe

There is a limit to how far we can see. The universe has a finite age, and light travels at a finite speed. We can only receive signals that have had enough time to reach us.

The region from which light has been able to reach us is called the **observable universe**. It is not necessarily all that exists. Space beyond that region may continue much farther, perhaps without an edge, but we cannot currently observe it directly.

The observable universe is also larger in radius than 13.8 billion light-years. That can sound strange: if the universe is about 13.8 billion years old, how can some of the matter whose light we see now be much farther away than 13.8 billion light-years? The answer is that space expanded while the light was travelling. The distance to the source today is not the same as the distance the light travelled through space.

## How do we investigate something we cannot visit?

Cosmology relies on several kinds of evidence. No telescope can travel back in time, but different observations give us independent clues.

### 1. Galaxies are moving apart

When astronomers study the light from many distant galaxies, they find that its wavelengths are stretched. This effect is called **redshift**. On large scales, more distant galaxies generally show greater redshift, a pattern that supports an expanding universe.

If the universe is expanding today, then in the past the average distance between galaxies was smaller. Running that history backwards leads to a hotter, denser early universe.

### 2. The universe has an ancient afterglow

The **cosmic microwave background**, or CMB, is radiation released when the universe became cool enough for electrons and atomic nuclei to form neutral atoms. Before that time, light was repeatedly scattered by free electrons, so the universe was opaque to it.

The CMB has travelled through space for almost the entire age of the universe. Today it fills the sky and has cooled to a temperature of about 2.7 kelvin. Tiny variations in its temperature reveal small differences in the density of the early universe.

### 3. The amounts of light elements fit the early-universe picture

The Big Bang model predicts that the first few minutes were hot enough for nuclear reactions to make light atomic nuclei. The predicted amounts of hydrogen, helium, and small traces of other light elements broadly agree with measurements. This is called **Big Bang nucleosynthesis**.

Each line of evidence answers a different part of the story. Together, they make the hot Big Bang model much stronger than an idea based on one observation alone.

## What can we actually see?

The oldest light we can observe directly is the CMB. It was released roughly 380,000 years after the expansion began. Before that, the universe was too hot and filled with charged particles that scattered light again and again.

This does not mean nothing existed before the CMB. It means ordinary light cannot show us that earlier period directly. Scientists investigate it using physics, mathematical models, and indirect clues preserved in later observations.

Gravitational waves may eventually provide another way to investigate extremely early events. Unlike light, gravitational waves can travel through matter that would scatter or block electromagnetic radiation. Detecting a primordial background would be a major discovery, but no confirmed detection of primordial gravitational waves has yet settled the question.

## Where does our knowledge become uncertain?

The further back we try to go, the more important it becomes to separate tested science from possible explanations.

General relativity describes gravity and the large-scale evolution of the universe with extraordinary success. Quantum theory describes the behaviour of matter and energy at very small scales. Near the earliest moments, both kinds of physics may be needed at once. A complete, experimentally confirmed theory of quantum gravity does not yet exist.

That is why responsible cosmology does not pretend to know every detail. Ideas such as cosmic inflation, a bounce before expansion, or a multiverse are studied in different ways, but they do not all have the same level of evidence. A useful question is always: what observation could support or rule out this idea?

## A useful way to think about scientific confidence

For this series, we will keep three categories separate:

- **Well established:** supported by several independent observations, such as cosmic expansion and the existence of the CMB.
- **Strong scientific models:** explanations that fit a wide range of evidence but still contain questions, such as the detailed physics of cosmic inflation.
- **Open questions:** subjects for which there is not yet a confirmed answer, including what happened at the earliest possible times.

This distinction does not make the universe less interesting. It makes the story more honest.

## Key takeaways

- The universe has been expanding and cooling for about 13.8 billion years.
- The observable universe is the part of the cosmos from which signals have had time to reach us.
- Galaxy redshifts, the cosmic microwave background, and the abundance of light elements support the hot Big Bang model.
- The CMB lets us observe the universe when it was about 380,000 years old, not at the exact beginning.
- The earliest moments remain an active area of research because our current theories are incomplete there.

## Think about it

If the oldest light we can directly observe comes from about 380,000 years after the beginning, what kinds of evidence could help scientists investigate an even earlier period?

*Image note: The JPL timeline image is an explanatory illustration, not a photograph of the Big Bang. The deep-field images are real telescope observations.*

title: The Big Bang
summary: The Big Bang is the scientific model of an expanding universe that began in a hot, dense state. Follow the evidence, the early timeline, and the common misunderstandings.
body:
## A universe with a history

The name “Big Bang” can create the wrong picture. It sounds like an explosion, perhaps with matter flying out from a central point. That is not what the modern model describes.

The Big Bang model says that the universe was once much hotter and denser than it is today. Space has expanded, the universe has cooled, and matter has gradually formed the structures we see: atoms, stars, galaxies, and planets.

The model does not describe an explosion into pre-existing empty space. In the standard picture, space itself expands. There is no known centre of the expansion that galaxies are all flying away from.

## How did the idea develop?

In the early twentieth century, astronomers began finding evidence that distant galaxies were generally moving away from us. In 1929, Edwin Hubble published a relation between the distances of galaxies and their recession speeds, building on earlier work by other scientists, including Georges Lemaître.

If the universe is expanding now, then it was smaller in the past. This led scientists to investigate a hot, dense early state. Over time, observations of the cosmic microwave background and the amounts of light elements gave the model strong support.

The name “Big Bang” was coined by astronomer Fred Hoyle during a radio broadcast in 1949. Hoyle himself favoured a different cosmological model at the time. The name stuck, even though it can be misleading.

## The evidence

A scientific model becomes convincing when it explains observations and makes predictions that can be checked. The Big Bang model is supported by several important lines of evidence.

### 1. The expansion of the universe

Light from many distant galaxies is shifted towards longer wavelengths. This is called **redshift**. For galaxies on large scales, greater distance generally goes with greater redshift.

The simplest explanation is that space has expanded while the light travelled. As space stretches, the wavelength of the light stretches too. This is not exactly the same as a car moving through air and changing the sound heard by a listener; it is the expansion of space that matters.

### 2. The cosmic microwave background

About 380,000 years after the universe began expanding, it had cooled enough for electrons to combine with nuclei and form neutral atoms. Light could then travel much more freely.

That ancient radiation is still around. As the universe expanded, its wavelength stretched and its temperature fell. Today we detect it as microwave radiation coming from every direction in the sky.

The CMB is not perfectly uniform. It contains tiny temperature differences, corresponding to small variations in the density of the early universe. Over billions of years, gravity helped those small differences grow into galaxies and larger structures.

![Planck map of the cosmic microwave background](https://planck.ipac.caltech.edu/system/avm_image_sqls/binaries/20/huge/planck13-002b.jpg?1366073607=)

*The Planck mission mapped tiny variations in the CMB. Image credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration. [Image details](https://planck.ipac.caltech.edu/image/planck13-002b).*

### 3. The first light elements

During the first few minutes, the universe was hot enough for protons and neutrons to combine into some of the lightest atomic nuclei. This process is called **Big Bang nucleosynthesis**.

The model predicts that most ordinary matter should have started as hydrogen, with a substantial amount of helium and tiny amounts of deuterium and lithium. Measurements of old, relatively unprocessed gas broadly match these predictions.

These three clues are powerful because they are different. Galaxy redshifts show expansion, the CMB is a remnant of the early hot universe, and light-element abundances preserve evidence of nuclear reactions in its first minutes.

## A short tour through cosmic history

The early universe changed quickly. The following timeline is simplified; the exact details of the earliest stages are still being studied.

- **The earliest moments:** The universe was extremely hot and dense. Our current theories do not yet give a complete description of the very first instant.
- **The first fractions of a second:** The universe expanded and cooled rapidly. Some models include a period of extremely rapid expansion called inflation, although its physical cause is not yet known.
- **The first few minutes:** Protons and neutrons formed light atomic nuclei, mostly hydrogen and helium nuclei.
- **About 380,000 years:** Electrons joined nuclei to form neutral atoms. The universe became transparent to light, and the CMB began its journey.
- **The first few hundred million years:** Gravity gathered gas into the first stars. Their light began to change the surrounding gas.
- **Later billions of years:** Galaxies grew, stars formed and died, and heavier elements were spread through space. Much later, our Solar System formed.

![NASA illustration of the story of the universe](https://d2pn8kiwq2w21t.cloudfront.net/original_images/infographicsuploadsinfographicsfull11147.jpg)

*An illustration of cosmic history from the early universe to the present. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech. [View the original infographic](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/infographics/the-story-of-our-universe/).*

## Was it an explosion?

This is probably the most common misunderstanding. An ordinary explosion sends fragments outward through space from a particular location. The Big Bang model is different: on very large scales, distances between unbound regions of space increase as space expands.

A helpful analogy is dots drawn on the surface of an inflating balloon. As the balloon grows, the distance between the dots increases, even though no dot is the centre of the surface. The analogy is limited: the universe is not known to be the surface of a balloon, and the analogy leaves out many dimensions and details. It only illustrates how distances can grow without a special centre on the surface.

## What happened before the Big Bang?

This is where we need to be careful. The standard model successfully describes the universe from a very early hot, dense state onward, but it does not settle every question about the ultimate beginning.

Some proposals suggest that our expanding universe emerged from an earlier contracting phase. Others explore whether the concept of “before” makes sense if time itself is part of the universe's history. These are research ideas, not established facts.

A good scientific explanation should tell us what evidence supports it and what future observation might test it. For now, the honest answer is that we do not know what, if anything, preceded the hot early universe.

## What the Big Bang model does not say

- It does not say that Earth or the Solar System was at the centre of the universe.
- It does not describe matter exploding into an already existing empty space.
- It does not explain, by itself, why the universe exists.
- It does not mean scientists have directly observed the exact first instant.
- It does not mean every detail of the early universe is settled.

## Key takeaways

- The Big Bang is a model of the universe's expansion from an earlier hot, dense state.
- The model is supported by galaxy redshifts, the CMB, and the observed abundance of light elements.
- The CMB was released when the universe was about 380,000 years old.
- The first stars formed much later, after a long period known as the cosmic dark ages.
- Questions about the earliest instant and any possible “before” remain open.

## Think about it

Why is the cosmic microwave background considered evidence for the Big Bang, rather than simply ordinary light from distant stars?

title: The Planck Epoch and the Limits of Physics
summary: A journey to the earliest times we can discuss with current physics, where gravity and quantum theory must meet and our best explanations are not yet complete.
body:
## Where our usual picture breaks down

Imagine rewinding the history of the universe. Galaxies move closer together. Atoms become impossible to keep intact. Nuclei break apart. Eventually, even the familiar idea of particles moving through smooth space and time becomes difficult to use.

The closer we get to the earliest moments, the more extreme the conditions become. To describe them properly, physicists need two very successful theories to work together: **general relativity**, our best description of gravity and spacetime on large scales, and **quantum mechanics**, which describes nature at very small scales.

The problem is that these theories have not yet been combined into a complete, experimentally confirmed theory of quantum gravity. That gap is one of the biggest challenges in fundamental physics.

## What is the Planck epoch?

The **Planck epoch** is the extremely early period of cosmic history, often described as the time before roughly (10^{-43}) seconds after the beginning of the hot Big Bang. The Planck time is about (5.39 	imes 10^{-44}) seconds.

That number is so small that it is difficult to build an everyday comparison for it. It is not a time interval that a laboratory clock can currently measure. It is a scale that appears when we combine fundamental constants to identify where quantum-gravity effects are expected to become important.

The Planck epoch is not a chapter of history that astronomers have directly photographed. It is a boundary where our current mathematical descriptions are expected to become incomplete.

## Why do we need quantum gravity?

General relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. It works extremely well for planets, stars, black holes, and the expansion of the universe.

Quantum theory, meanwhile, is essential for describing atoms, particles, and the forces that act at very small scales. It has passed many precise experimental tests.

In the earliest universe, the density and energy were so high that gravity may also have needed a quantum description. Using general relativity alone can lead to mathematical quantities becoming infinite in certain extrapolations. Such infinities are often a warning that a theory is being pushed beyond the conditions where it can be trusted.

Physicists are working on possible ways to describe quantum gravity. String theory and loop quantum gravity are two research approaches, among others. Neither has yet been confirmed as the final description of nature.

## What can we say about the Planck time?

It is tempting to say that nothing can be known before the Planck time. That is too strong. The more careful statement is that our established theories do not provide a reliable, complete description of that regime.

The Planck time is sometimes described as the smallest meaningful unit of time. That wording can be misleading. It is a natural scale in physics, not proof that time comes in tiny indivisible ticks. Whether time is continuous, discrete, or something more complicated at the deepest level remains unknown.

It is also not certain that the universe had a simple first moment in the everyday sense. Some models explore a bounce from an earlier phase, while others examine how time could emerge from a more fundamental description. These ideas are mathematically interesting, but they are not settled observations.

## What might have happened after this era?

Once the universe expanded and cooled enough for our known physics to become more useful, the story becomes easier to describe. The early universe passed through stages in which fundamental particles and forces behaved differently from the familiar world today.

Some cosmological models include **cosmic inflation**: a proposed period of extremely rapid expansion very early in the universe's history. Inflation can help explain why the observable universe looks so similar in different directions and how tiny initial variations could have become the seeds of later cosmic structure.

However, the exact mechanism behind inflation is unknown, and scientists are still searching for decisive observational evidence. It is important not to confuse a useful model with a fully solved mystery.

## Can telescopes show us the Planck epoch?

Not directly. The oldest electromagnetic signal we can observe is the cosmic microwave background, released when the universe was about 380,000 years old. That is enormously later than the Planck epoch.

Still, observations can test ideas about earlier times indirectly. Scientists study the pattern of temperature variations in the CMB, the distribution of galaxies, and the possible signatures of primordial gravitational waves. Different theories can predict different patterns.

A future detection could rule out some models or make others more plausible. But a signal must be checked carefully: foreground radiation, instrument effects, and other astrophysical sources can imitate the pattern researchers are looking for.

![Planck map of the cosmic microwave background](https://planck.ipac.caltech.edu/system/avm_image_sqls/binaries/20/huge/planck13-002b.jpg?1366073607=)

*The CMB is a much later snapshot of the universe, not an image of the Planck epoch. Its tiny variations help scientists test models of the early cosmos. Credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration. [Image details](https://planck.ipac.caltech.edu/image/planck13-002b).*

## The difference between a calculation and a discovery

A mathematical model can be consistent and still not describe the real universe. To become part of established science, it needs to make predictions that can be tested against observations or experiments.

That is why the Planck epoch is such an interesting subject. Physicists can calculate what happens when they combine known constants, explore different theories, and look for possible observational consequences. But they cannot honestly claim to know exactly what happened during this era.

The unknowns are not a weakness of science. They show where new ideas and better evidence are needed.

## Key takeaways

- The Planck epoch refers to an extremely early regime, around the Planck time of (5.39 	imes 10^{-44}) seconds.
- General relativity and quantum theory are both important, but a complete tested theory of quantum gravity is still missing.
- The Planck time is a physical scale, not proof that time is made of indivisible ticks.
- Cosmic inflation is an influential proposal, but its physical cause and detailed mechanism remain uncertain.
- Telescopes cannot directly photograph the Planck epoch; researchers look for indirect evidence in later cosmic signals.

## Think about it

If a theory makes a beautiful mathematical prediction but no observation can test it, what would scientists need before treating it as a reliable description of the universe?

- NASA/JPL-Caltech, [The Story of Our Universe](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/infographics/the-story-of-our-universe/). Overview of the universe's history.
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, [Quantum Gravity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/quantum-gravity/). Background on the open theoretical problem.

*The Planck epoch is a theoretical regime, not an observed photograph. The CMB image is included to show one of the later observations used to test early-universe models.*
